claims.text: The target material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The specimen has nominally similar microstructure across the two measured temperature regimes.
The proposed machine-learning framework will combine experimentally measured oxygen effects with ab initio or analytical defect-scattering data.
Machine-learning models can be trained using first-principles data for refractory complex concentrated alloys.
Predictions will cover nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Nominally pure HfNbTaTiZr references will be compared with the 1 wt.% oxygen specimen.
Oxygen produces point defects in HfNbTaTiZr.
The oxygen-induced point defects scatter both phonons and electrons.
Defect-related scattering changes thermal transport relative to an ideal-crystal model.
Chemically and topologically disordered alloys can exhibit thermal transport dominated by the electronic contribution, with a comparatively small phononic contribution.
Representing actual lattice disorder and oxygen content will improve thermal-conductivity prediction fidelity over purely analytical methods.
Existing analytical thermal-conductivity approaches for HfNbTaTiZr assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Analytical approaches that ignore dopant and defect effects show larger discrepancies for oxygen-bearing samples.
Current analytical predictions typically deviate by 5–10% in the stated temperature regimes.
The proposed model will improve prediction accuracy by more than the cited 5–10% deviation.
The proposed model's advantage will be especially pronounced at low temperatures because defect scattering notably affects transport there.
Applicability is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and microstructures similar to those represented in training.
Extrapolation to substantially higher oxygen contents or markedly different alloy compositions remains unvalidated.
Model accuracy may vary with microstructure, measurement uncertainty, and training-data coverage.
A deviation exceeding 5% beyond measurement error at any benchmark temperature will falsify the hypothesis.
